subject: Spatial modeling dependent on start and end location (flow)

messages.author: 402404e6aea6ffb8
messages.subject: Spatial modeling dependent on start and end location (flow)
parts:
I was wondering if there has been any work in calculating spatial values based on where each observation starts in a given mesh and where it ends up, essentially the origin/destination are both informative in predicting the value. An example of this might be measuring the cost of transportation from Boston to Denver vs. Atlanta to Denver vs. Boston to Dallas. In each of these examples, both the origin and destination location is important but there is also some correlation with Boston to Denver having a similar cost to Boston to Boulder Colorado. I haven't been able to find any documentation that could handle this sort of problem and would appreciate any suggestions.

Thanks!

messages.author: a8355c7795288f3f
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial modeling dependent on start and end location (flow)
parts: I'm not sure what kind of 'spatial values' you're looking for. If you're asking about (network) flow model measurements (e.g. shortest paths, , as it is called in combinatorial optimization problems (discrete math, linear optimization, integer optimization etc.), then you would need to apply linear/integer optimization solutions (e.g. shortest paths, p-medians, network partitioning etc.). Convexity, manifolds (e.g. locally Euclidean spaces) etc. cannot be assumed in such network flow settings ... Regards, Rudy

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial modeling dependent on start and end location (flow)
parts: I am not looking for any optimization, but predictions based on historic data. These prediction (transportation costs) have a spatial correlational component that I am trying to capture with INLA and SPDE methods. It appears that the methods can easily produce a 2d "heat map" of prediction for a given spatial area if I keep the origin constant. However, I would like to allow the origin of these transportation costs to vary to create a more complex correlation mapping.
